nodes.label: Management
nodes.question: How have Australian conservation practitioners responded to the shortfall in government-led conservation efforts?
nodes.answer: They have sought to acquire and manage vast areas across the continent to conserve threatened species and enhance the representativeness of the conservation estate.
nodes.paragraph: 2019). The threats to Australia S biodiversity are pervasive and are driving an extinction crisis unparalleled among similarly wealthy nations. The creation of protected areas has done little to redress the rapid post-colonial impacts of habitat loss from land clearing and fragmentation (Ward et al. 2019), predation by introduced species (i.e. cats and foxes) that native fauna is not adapted to avoid (Harrison et al. 2023) and inappropriate fire regimes (Doherty et al. 2024). In recognition of the urgent need to respond, the private or non-governmental organisation (NGO)-led protected area model, popular in the United Kingdom, Southern Africa and South America, has burgeoned only recently in Australia (post-2010). Australian conservation practitioners have sought to redress the shortfall in the government-led response to conserve threatened species and enhance representative- ness of the conservation estate through acquisition and management of vast areas across the continent (Fitzsimons 2015; Ivanova and Cook 2020). While there is the growing network of large conservation reserves under the ownership and management of large NGOs such as Bush Heritage or Animal Wildlife Conservancy (Fitzsimons 2015), myriad opportunities persist for conservation action on smaller par - cels of private land (Cannon 1999; Kearney et al.

To date, modelling techniques have not taken trait data into account. Natural history traits and how they interact with environmental parameters and influ- ence species abundance can inform conservation manage- ment. The interaction between ecological and trait data is termed the fourth corner (Brown et al. 2014), the advent of fourth corner techniques allows the modelling of abundance data in relation to observed ecological data and recorded trait data, as well as abundance as a function of the interac- tion between ecological and trait data. Recently, it has been recognized that not only are trait data essential for informing the conservation of species, but also that there is a paucity of trait data available for amphibians and reptiles (Etard et al. 2020). Although habitat loss affects all taxonomic groups, carnivores are particularly vul- nerable given their low fecundity, high habitat area requirements and high vulnerability to human persecution (Cardillo et al. 2004). nodes.question: How many species and subspecies of samphires are recorded in Australia, and what is their conservation status?
nodes.answer: There are 58 species and 19 subspecies of samphires recorded in Australia, with two federally listed as threatened, eight having formal conservation listings in at least one state or territory, and 25 recognized as data deficient or priority taxa.

Turner2 Grant Palmer1 Singarayer Florentine1,3 Received: 22 December 2023 / Revised: 17 January 2025 / Accepted: 10 February 2025 The Author(s) 2025 Abstract Australia is home to a rich assemblage of samphires (Tecticornia and Salicornia spp.) which are largely endemic, inhabiting saline and semi-saline areas across climatically diverse regions. While these plants are adapted to harsh conditions, they are vulnerable to the effects of climate change which is anticipated to exacerbate existing management and environmental pressures. Despite the threatened and priority status of many samphires, there is an overall lack of knowledge surrounding their distribution, ecology and responses to environmental threats, data which we believe is critical to support their conservation and management. We have compiled and critically assessed peer-reviewed and online grey lit- erature and databases to provide an overview of threatened and poorly known samphires in Australia, with particular reference to their distribution, threats and ecological responses.

Additionally, many species are yet to be formally evaluated against the Interna- tional Union for the Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List threat categories, despite likely meeting the criteria (Le Breton et al. 2019). The number of data-deficient plant spe- cies is also increasing in some regions with the discovery of new, yet undescribed taxa, adding to the backlog of species with inadequate data to assess their conservation status (Gosper et al. 2022). To prevent further decline, it is essential to identify species most at threat or considered poorly known, and gather data to underpin management and conser - vation efforts. Whilst samphire species (Tecticornia Hook.f. and Salicornia L. spp. : Sali- cornioideae Ulbr. : Chenopodiaceae/Amaranthaceae clade) are widespread globally, Aus- tralian species are largely endemic and little is known about most of them. Although many are recognised as threatened, priority or data-deficient, few have specific management plans to assist with their conservation. Samphires are stem-succulent, halophytic plants that occur across a range of saline and semi-saline habitats, from coastal saltmarshes in varied climates to inland salt lakes and saline flats within rangelands of arid and semi-arid regions (Department of the Envi- ronment and Energy [DEE] 2017).

nodes.paragraph: These communities provide ecological benefits such as filtering runoff to marine areas, and habitat for birds and many other species including rare and threatened taxa (DEE 2017). Samphires also contribute to soil stabilisation, range- land pastoral production, ecotourism and biodiversity conservation (Williams 2002; DEE 2017), and are utilised both as a human food source and for medicinal purposes (Srivara- than et al. 2021). While samphires are considered robust plants due to their ability to thrive and grow in harsh conditions, they are adapted to specific and often narrow environmental niches which make them vulnerable to changes in those conditions (Datson 2002). Their distribution is largely influenced by fluctuations in salinity, water availability and tempera- ture, with their survival determined by tolerances to extreme conditions (Koull & Chehma 2014; Chenchouni 2017; Contreras-Cruzado et al. 2017). As salinity and waterlogging lev - els change rapidly with variations in hydrology, salt lakes are particularly vulnerable to the effects of climate change (Jellison et al. 2008). Recent reports by the Intergovernmen- tal Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) (2022) indicate arid climate zones are highly vulner - able to climate change and have been affected globally, influenced by intermittent rainfall and increased temperatures.

Exogenous environmental stressors such as extreme temperatures can impose thresholds for essential ecological functions such as seed germination (Cochrane 2020). The effects of these stress- ors are uncertain in the face of climate change, particularly for species already under threat or with restricted distributions (Elliott et al. 2019; Cochrane 2020), or those with specific environmental requirements (Broadhurst & Coates 2017). Adding to the complexity is that while suitable habitats may contract for some samphire species with climate change (Cole- man 2024), new habitats may become available for other halophytes with the expansion of saline and arid lands. Therefore, it remains important to identify and protect species most at risk of changing conditions. Whilst the intraspecific variability of these traits has implications for individuals, population dynamics and evolution (Schupp et al. 2019; Snell et al. 2019), responses to varying environmental conditions among different populations is not well understood, par - ticularly for different life stages (Cochrane et al. 2015).
